claims.text: The FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a single-phase solid-solution microstructure with a typical cast/dislocation structure.
Removing Co causes mechanically induced short-range ordering to begin earlier during deformation than in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Dynamic strain-induced short-range ordering pins dislocations and modifies the dislocation structure.
Co removal changes solute-dislocation interaction energies.
The change in solute-dislocation interaction energy lowers the barrier to mechanically induced short-range ordering.
Short-range ordering hinders dislocation glide at lower strains or temperatures.
Suppression of glide forces an earlier transition to dislocation climb and dynamic recovery or recrystallization.
The transition toward climb and dynamic recovery or recrystallization underpins the alloy's favorable strength-ductility balance.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has a well-established strength-ductility response suitable as a baseline.
The relevant test regime extends from cryogenic temperatures to about 600 °C and from approximately 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-2 s^-1.
Diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated mechanisms are active throughout the stated temperature and strain-rate regime.
The Co-free alloy remains a stable single-phase solid solution throughout the stated testing regime.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will show an earlier onset of increased strain hardening.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, the Co-free alloy will show higher apparent activation energies for dislocation motion.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit microstructural signatures of short-range order and modified dislocation arrangements during deformation.
Dynamic recrystallization or nanoscale precipitation may contribute concurrently to the observed behavior.
A controlled temperature- and strain-rate matrix comparing Co-free FeNiCrMn directly with equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi can test the proposed mechanism.
Temperature-dependent mechanical testing can be used to estimate apparent activation energies and assess a possible climb-controlled regime.
Failure to observe both an earlier strain-hardening onset and dynamic short-range-order signatures in the Co-free alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
